<<Atkinson's Maiden Century at Lord's>>

The morning sun cast long shadows across the hallowed turf of Lord's as Gus Atkinson strode to the crease on day two. The weight of expectation that should have crushed him after a sleepless night simply wasn't there. His teammates had worried needlessly about him through the evening, imagining him tossing and turning in his hotel bed, mentally replaying every possible scenario. But Atkinson had slept like a baby, his mind clear and focused on the task ahead.

From the very first delivery, it was evident that the overnight break had done nothing to disturb his rhythm. The ball from Kumara was dispatched with casual elegance, racing to the boundary as if guided by invisible hands. His cover drive that followed was textbook perfection, the kind that coaching manuals are built around. The Sri Lankan bowlers looked increasingly desperate, their field placements becoming more defensive with each passing over.

The close call with the lbw decision could have rattled a lesser player. The umpire's finger went up, and for a moment, the dream seemed to slip away. But Atkinson's confident review proved correct, technology vindicating his judgment as the ball tracking showed it missing leg stump comfortably. His teammates' celebrations on the balcony reflected the collective relief and renewed optimism.

Chain reactions of poor bowling and brilliant batting continued to unfold. Sri Lanka's bowlers, already demoralized from the previous evening's punishment, served up a buffet of loose deliveries. Atkinson feasted accordingly, each boundary stroke more authoritative than the last. The outfield, quick as lightning under the summer sun, seemed to accelerate the ball even further, turning good shots into great ones.

When the moment finally arrived, it was almost anticlimactic in its simplicity. A drive past mid-off brought up the magical three figures - 103 runs from 103 balls. The crowd rose as one, acknowledging a special innings from a special talent. His final pull shot, dripping with disdain for Kumara's attempted bouncer, was the exclamation point on a morning that belonged entirely to him.
